\title{Diagnose, Fix, Measure: An Applied Study of a Database-and-Documents Assistant, and Where a Cheap
Decision Model Can Replace LLM Calls}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Author names (placeholder)}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Affiliation (placeholder)\\ email (placeholder)}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We report an applied study of StateSync, an assistant that answers questions from a company's SQL database, its
uploaded filings, or both. On FinanceBench's open sample the shipped system answered \N{fbShip} of
\N{fbN} questions correctly. A diagnosis traced most failures to two design flaws: a router that saw only the 20
most recent document titles and nothing of the database, and an answer writer that read the first 8 of 25
retrieved passages in document order. Fixing the design flaws raised accuracy on this development set to
\N{fbBge}, and on a held-out
routing test a single front-door LLM call routed \N{rtLLMAcc} of questions correctly against \N{rtShipAcc} for the shipped
router. For SQL answers, falling back to a pool of candidates when a small trained verifier doubts the first
answer raised execution accuracy on \N{sN} held-out BIRD questions from \N{sFirst} to \N{sPsix}
(pre-registered, \N{sH3P}). Across both parts we test a hosted decision model, Jev, as a cheap replacement for LLM
calls. Used zero-shot it detects wrong SQL answers nearly as well as an LLM judge (AUROC \N{sAurocJev} vs
\N{sAurocJudge}). Asked one choice question, it routes about as accurately as the LLM front door (\N{rtJevCAcc} vs \N{rtLLMrawAcc},
no significant difference) with no LLM call. In a
pre-registered test on \N{pgN} held-out questions it puts the right filing page first \N{pgJBFirst} of the time,
against \N{pgBFirst} for a cross-encoder re-ranker. Used as independent yes/no
decisions, it cannot express that a question needs both sources. We report the negative results alongside the
positive ones.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
text-to-SQL, retrieval-augmented generation, query routing, verification, decision models, evaluation
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Assistants that answer business questions increasingly sit in front of two kinds of source at once: a
database of figures and a library of documents. Such a system has to decide where a question should go, find
the right passage or write the right query, and know when its own answer is likely wrong. Each of these
decisions is usually made by another large language model (LLM) call. Each call adds seconds and cost, and
each can fail in its own way.

This paper reports what happened when we measured one such system, StateSync, honestly rather than on the
questions it was built around. The shipped system answered \N{fbShip} of FinanceBench's open questions
\cite{islam2023financebench} correctly. We traced the failures to concrete design flaws, fixed them, and
measured every fix against a baseline. Where we had used a question set to find a flaw, we built a fresh,
held-out set to confirm the fix, and fixed its analysis plan before any data existed. Throughout, we ask
one further question: which of the system's LLM calls can a cheap decision model replace? We use Jev
\cite{typesafe2026jev}, which answers typed yes/no and choice questions about a given state with
probabilities, writes no text, and costs a fraction of a cent per call.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A diagnosis and its fixes.} We show how a blind router and a passage-ordering choice cost most of
a document assistant's accuracy, and how fixing them raises FinanceBench accuracy from \N{fbShip} to
\N{fbBge}. A single front-door call replaces three LLM calls before routing.
\item \textbf{Detect-then-fallback for SQL.} On \N{sN} held-out BIRD questions \cite{li2023bird}, a trained
verifier's doubt about the first answer triggers a fallback to a pool of 21 candidate queries, raising
execution accuracy from \N{sFirst} to \N{sPsix} (pre-registered, confirmed after Holm correction). Two other pre-registered hypotheses were not confirmed.
\item \textbf{A decision model as a cheap layer.} Jev replaces an LLM judge for flagging wrong SQL answers at
some loss (AUROC \N{sAurocJev} vs \N{sAurocJudge}). Asked one choice question, it replaces the LLM router
(\N{rtJevCAcc} vs \N{rtLLMrawAcc}, no significant difference). In a pre-registered held-out test it moves the right
page to the top of the retrieved passages \N{pgJBFirst} vs \N{pgBFirst} of the time. It fails when its decisions
are posed as independent yes/no questions.
\item \textbf{Negative results, reported.} A ``not answerable'' reply for SQL missed its pre-set bar for false
refusals. The fixed system did not significantly beat the shipped one on held-out two-source questions. A
conformal ``verified'' label never reached usable coverage.
\end{itemize}
